questions.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t=3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}[3f(t)-g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{4}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,-6,\,3⟩-⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,4,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,-10,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\text{d}t={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[f(t)-\frac{3}{2}g(t)]\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-\frac{3}{2}⟨1,\,-2,\,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,6,\,-1⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2}\,-3,\,-9⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,9,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}[f(t)-3g(t)]\,\text{d}t={\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-3{\int }_{2}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}[f(t)-3g(t)]\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-3{\int }_{2}^{3}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨2,\,-4,\,-2⟩-3⟨1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-4,\,-2⟩-⟨3,\,6,\,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,-10,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨4,\,-10,\,-14⟩ \\  & =⟨-4,\,10,\,14⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the scalar multiplication rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot ⟨-4,\,10,\,14⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,5,\,7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\,-1,\,-\frac{3}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the scalar multiplication rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}4f(t)\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{2},\,-1,\,-\frac{3}{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,-4,\,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨1,\,-3,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the scalar multiplication rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2f(t)\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,-2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,6,\,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,9,\,6⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-9,\,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, applying the scalar multiplication rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot ⟨3,\,-9,\,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-3,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,6,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-6,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{0}f(t)+⟨3,\,1,\,-2⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{4}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{0}⟨3,\,1,\,-2⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨3,\,-6,\,0⟩+⟨3t,\,t,\,-2t⟩{|}_{4}^{0} \\  & =⟨3,\,-6,\,0⟩+⟨-12,\,-4,\,8⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨-9,\,-10,\,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{6}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨8,\,-6,\,15⟩-⟨-2,\,3,\,4⟩ \\  & =⟨10,\,-9,\,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{4}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨5,\,1,\,20⟩-⟨1,\,1,\,8⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,0,\,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t-(-{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨2,\,4,\,-10⟩+⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,6,\,-11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{3}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{5}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{5}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-4,\,-12,\,14⟩-⟨2,\,8,\,-8⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,12,\,-14⟩-⟨2,\,8,\,-8⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,4,\,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the adjacent intervals rule, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-16,\,8,\,-32⟩-⟨2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨14,\,-6,\,31⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i+j-k)\times (4\,i+2\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 4 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(2-0)i-(2+4)j+(0-4)k \\  & =2i-6j-4k.\end{aligned}
$$

The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(-i+j+3\,k)\cdot (16\,i-10\,j+4\,k) \\  & =-16-10+12 \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{2}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-2\,j+2\,k)\times (6\,i-4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 6 & -4 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -4 & 3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 6 & 3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-6+8)i-(3-12)j+(-4+12)k \\  & =2\,i+9\,j+8\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{3}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i-j+2\,k)\times (i+j-3\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(3-2)i-(-3-2)j+(1+1)k \\  & =i+5\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that 
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t=\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\,i+\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k,$ 
$c=i+u\,j-\frac{\pi }{4}\,k,$
and 
${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ what is the value of $u?$
questions.worked_solution:
The dot product rule states that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Applying the dot-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(i+u\,j-\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)\cdot (\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}\,i+\,j+\frac{\pi }{2}\,k) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8}+u-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}c\cdot f(t)\,\text{d}t=0,$ we must have $u=0.$

canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} [  3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) ] \,\textrm{d}t$ given that $\displaystyle{\int_0^2} \mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 16, \: 2,\: -2\right\rangle$ and $\displaystyle{\int_0^2}\mathbf g(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 2,-4,2\right\rangle .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
From the vector addition and scalar multiplication rules, we have

$$
\displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \big[ \, 3 \mathbf f(t)+\mathbf g(t) \, \big] \, \textrm d t =  \displaystyle {3\int_0^2 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t + \displaystyle {\int_0^2 } \mathbf g(t) \, \textrm d t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}[3f(t)+g(t)]\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3⟨16,\,2,\,-2⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨48,\,6,\,-6⟩+⟨2,\,-4,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨50,2,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨t,\,-t,\,t⟩{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨2,\,-2,\,2⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨5,\,-4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Calculate 
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$
given that
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, \: 1, \: 3 \right\rangle$
and
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 0, \: 2, \: 6 \right\rangle.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the adjacent intervals, we get

$$
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t+\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t .
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t = 
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t - \int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\displaystyle {\int_0^1 }  \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t)  \, \textrm d t$ 
given that 
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm d t = \mathbf i-3\,\mathbf j-4\,\mathbf k$ 
and 
$\mathbf c=\mathbf j-\mathbf k .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int_0^1 } \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t =  \mathbf c \times {\int_0^1 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t  .
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(j-k)\times (i-3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-4-3)i-(0+1)j+(0-1)k \\  & =-7\,i-\,j-\,k.\end{aligned}
$$
